chapter_theme: Oppressive rule as a crime and a self-destruction: the king who extorts is a murderer and a highwayman, and his people's tears wear away his wealth. Its effects reach everything, turning wealth into a burden, and in the older reading failing the rain, the cows and the sacred books.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar's divisions: the fault of oppression (551-552), what the oppressor suffers (553-556), what those under him suffer (557-558), and what befalls his land (559-560).

551.reading: A king who takes up harassing people and goes on doing wrong is crueller than those who have taken up murder.
551.nuance: Both are given the same verb மேற்கொண்டு, taken up as a trade. Parimelazhagar's reason concerns duration: the killer's harm is for a moment, the oppressor's all the time. He adds the reason is wanting wealth.

552.reading: The asking of one who stands with a sceptre is like one standing with a spear saying 'hand it over'.
552.nuance: The cutting word is இரவு: the king is begging, or calls it that. A request backed by the power to punish isn't a request. Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar agree that this is about demands beyond the fixed dues. Manakkudavar adds it is like robbery even when worded as a request.

553.reading: A ruler who doesn't examine daily and do justice loses his land day by day.
553.nuance: The repeated நாடொறும், and the play of நாடி and நாடு, make the decline as gradual as the neglect. Parimelazhagar notes two ways to read it: that the king loses the land's fruits or that the land itself decays.

554.reading: A ruler who bends the sceptre and acts without reflection loses resources and people together.
554.nuance: சூழாது is the failure here, not malice. Pope's 'who counsel doth refuse' is more specific than the Tamil. Parimelazhagar makes the people the source of future wealth, so a bad king loses past and future income at a stroke.

555.reading: Are not the tears shed by those who can't bear their affliction the weapon that wears away wealth?
555.nuance: தேய்க்கும் is slow wearing: tears work like an abrasive. Parimelazhagar sees a saw and a tree in it, and says the real agent is the sin of causing affliction, shifted onto the tears. So he supplies a moral mechanism the verse leaves unstated. Kalaignar has the tears destroy the regime, though the verse says wealth.

556.reading: For rulers, enduring is by just rule; without it, the lustre of rulers doesn't endure.
556.nuance: The verse plays on மன்னர், மன்னுதல், மன்னா, ruler and enduring in one root, as if a ruler is by definition one who lasts. Parimelazhagar takes ஒளி as fame and adds the implication that the ruler himself doesn't endure.

557.reading: As the lack of rain is to the earth, so the king's lack of tender regard is to those who live.
557.nuance: The negative of 542, as Parimelazhagar points out. But note the shift: 542 needs the sceptre, and 557 fears the lack of அளி, kindness. The failure of a king here is one of feeling as well as of law.

558.reading: Under the sceptre of a ruler who doesn't do justice, having is more painful than having nothing.
558.nuance: Pope's couplet, adding a sting to poverty, misses this, though his gloss has it. Parimelazhagar spells out the reason with grim realism: only those who have something get shackled and tortured for it.

559.reading: If the ruler bends justice in what he does, the sky, bending the rain, won't pour.
559.nuance: கோடி is used of both king and cloud, so the same bending passes between them, and the grammar itself does the work of linking them.

positions.position: It is literal: rain in fact fails to come in season, and the next verse gives the cause.
positions.quote: அவன் நாட்டுப் பருவமழை இன்றாம் வகை மேகம் பொழிதலைச் செய்யாது.

positions.position: It is a practical chain: bad government lets reservoirs fall into ruin, so rain can't be stored.
positions.quote: நீரைத் தேக்கிப் பயனளிக்கும் இடங்கள் பாழ்பட்டுப் போகுமாதலால்,

560.reading: If the guardian doesn't guard, the yield of cows declines and those of the six occupations forget their books.

positions.position: Those of the six duties are Brahmins. Without milk and mantras there is no sacrifice, and that is why rain fails, which completes 559.
positions.quote: பசுக்கள் பால் குன்றியவழி அவியின்மையானும், அது கொடுத்தற்குரியார் மந்திரம் கற்பம் என்பன ஓதாமையானும், வேள்வி நடவாதாம்;

positions.position: They are not a caste: the verse means that productive work and key occupations dwindle.
positions.quote: ஆக்கப்பணிகள் எதுவும் நடக்காது; முக்கியமான தொழில்களும் தேய்ந்து விடும்.

links.note: 546 says it isn't the spear but the sceptre that wins. 552 collapses the difference: a sceptre that asks is a spear. The same pair, வேல் and கோல், marks the line between justice and its corruption.

550 has a king kill the cruel as weeds. The very next verse calls an oppressive king crueller than killers. My reading: read together, the two raise the question 550 leaves open, of who weeds the weeder, and the chapter's answer is tears, rain and time.

659 says what was taken with tears departs with tears. 555 makes the same moral arithmetic political. 659 is a personal warning about money, and here the crying of a whole people is the weapon against a throne.

1041 says nothing is more painful than poverty except poverty itself. 558 names something more painful: wealth under a tyrant. The later chapter's superlative doesn't hold in this one's political conditions.

A mirror: just rule brings rain and harvest in 545, and bent rule stops the rain in 559. Kalaignar rationalises both, a comparison in one and reservoirs in the other, because the older reading asks a modern reader to believe in moral weather.

543 makes the sceptre the origin of books and virtue, and 560 shows the effect of its absence: the books are forgotten. Parimelazhagar's chain then connects these to rain through sacrifice, which ties 11, 543 and 559 into one circle.
